Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has shown a partial radiologic response with disappearance of three lesions and ≥40 % shrinkage of the remaining lesions, suggesting that conversion to resectability may be feasible. However, definitive assessment of hepatic resectability requires specific information that is not provided (exact number, size, and segmental distribution of the residual lesions, relationship to major vascular structures, and calculated future liver remnant). Because this missing data is decisive for planning a curative hepatectomy, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the required evaluation.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOXIRI or an alternative regimen such as FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for at least 2–3 additional cycles to maximize tumor shrinkage and to allow further assessment of response.  
- Perform a high‑resolution, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or liver‑specific PET/CT) within 4–6 weeks to delineate the exact number, size, and segmental location of the residual lesions, and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).  
- If the FLR is projected to be <30 % in a normal liver (or <40 % in a chemotherapy‑injured liver), plan a pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
- Re‑stage the liver surgery based on the imaging:  
   • If all remaining lesions can be encompassed within a single anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with adequate margins (≥1 cm) and sufficient FLR, schedule a one‑stage curative hepatectomy.  
   • If lesions are bilobar and cannot be cleared safely in one operation, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in one lobe with PVE of the contralateral lobe; second stage: resection of the hypertrophied lobe).  
- Simultaneously address the primary rectal tumor:  
   • If the primary lesion is still locally advanced, give long‑course chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) after systemic therapy is completed.  
   • If the primary has responded or is low‑risk, consider synchronous resection (combined colorectal and hepatic surgery) only after confirming hepatic resectability and patient fitness.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of FOLFOXIRI or switch to a maintenance regimen) for at least 3 months, guided by pathological response and molecular profile (RAS/BRAF status).  
- Enroll the patient in a clinical trial or consider hepatic‑directed therapies (e.g., radiofrequency ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy) for any residual lesions that are not amenable to resection.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact number, size, and segmental distribution of the residual liver lesions after chemotherapy.  
- Relationship of residual lesions to major hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and hepatic artery branches.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and liver function tests (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, coagulation profile).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Current status of the primary rectal tumor (clinical T/N stage, response to any prior radiotherapy, distance from anal verge).  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and baseline cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Trends in tumor markers (CEA) beyond the baseline value.
Reference:

The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

The two recommendations are substantially similar across all evaluated criteria:

1. **Completeness:** Both recommendations address major clinical domains such as resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy. They both discuss the use of systemic chemotherapy, the need for high-resolution imaging, and strategies to assess and optimize liver resectability, as well as potential postoperative therapies.

2. **Step-by-step Concordance:** Both recommendations classify the liver metastases as 'potentially resectable' and stress the need for further detailed evaluation before proceeding with definitive surgical plans. They propose similar management plans, including continuation of chemotherapy, advanced imaging, and detailed restaging before surgical decisions, indicating alignment in key clinical reasoning steps.

3. **Case-tailoring Concordance:** Both recommendations consider patient-specific factors such as the molecular profile, lesion-specific surgical considerations, and strategies tailored to the individual's response to treatment. They also emphasize the importance of the primary tumor's status and individual tumor marker trends, suggesting a tailored approach based on specific case details.

4. **Missing Data Concordance:** Both recommendations identify similar critical missing information, including the exact location and segmentation of lesions, future liver remnant calculations, and the status of the primary tumor. They both stress the need for molecular profiling and comprehensive imaging data to inform further management decisions. This demonstrates alignment in recognizing the essential missing clinical data required for further management.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: After 4 cycles of chemotherapy the number of hepatic lesions has decreased from ten to three, each <2 cm, suggesting a good radiologic response. However, resectability hinges on (a) the anatomical distribution of the three lesions (unilobar vs bilobar, proximity to major vascular structures) and (b) the anticipated future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve. These decisive pieces of information are not provided, therefore definitive upfront resection cannot be confirmed at this time.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy to consolidate response: complete a total of 6–8 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS wild‑type status, unless contraindicated.  
- Re‑image the liver (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) after the additional cycles to reassess lesion size, number, and distribution; perform volumetric analysis to calculate FLR.  
- Evaluate the rectal primary: obtain high‑resolution pelvic MRI and endoscopic assessment to stage the tumor, determine response to chemotherapy, and decide whether neoadjuvant chemoradiation is required before any surgical intervention.  
- If imaging confirms that all hepatic disease can be cleared with an adequate FLR (≥30 % in a normal liver, ≥40 % in a steatotic or chemotherapy‑injured liver), plan curative‑intent liver resection.  
   • Prefer parenchymal‑sparing resections (segmentectomy or wedge) to preserve liver volume.  
   • If FLR is borderline, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) as appropriate.  
- Coordinate timing of rectal surgery:  
   • If the rectal tumor is locally advanced (cT3‑4 or N+), deliver long‑course chemoradiation followed by a waiting interval, then perform either a simultaneous colorectal‑liver resection (if technically feasible and patient condition allows) or a staged approach (liver first, then rectal resection).  
   • If the rectal lesion is early (cT1‑2, N0) and asymptomatic, consider deferring rectal surgery until after hepatic resection, provided oncologic safety is not compromised.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: after R0 liver resection and definitive treatment of the primary, resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months total) to address micrometastatic disease.  
- Throughout, maintain close multidisciplinary surveillance with serial CEA measurements and imaging every 2–3 months.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Precise hepatic lesion locations (segmental distribution, relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary structures).  
- Quantitative liver function assessment (Child‑Pugh, indocyanine‑green clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelet count) and volumetric FLR calculation.  
- Performance status and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Current staging of the rectal primary (MRI T/N stage, distance from mesorectal fascia, presence of mesorectal nodes).  
- Response of the primary tumor to chemotherapy (clinical, endoscopic, radiologic).  
- Need for, and timing of, neoadjuvant radiotherapy for the rectal cancer.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants, distant lymph nodes).  
- Details of prior chemotherapy regimen, cumulative oxaliplatin exposure, and any signs of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Completeness: Both recommendations are comprehensive regarding the major clinical domains and management components, such as systemic therapy continuation, imaging for re-assessment, and planning of surgical interventions. They both address the importance of liver function and remnant calculations, consider the management of the rectal primary tumor, and include postoperative therapy.

Step-by-step concordance: There is a lack of concordance in how resectability is assessed. Recommendation 1 states that resectability is potentially achievable but cannot be confirmed yet due to missing anatomical details, whereas Recommendation 2 considers the situation resectable pending reassessment. The management plans also differ: Recommendation 1 suggests continuing chemotherapy and reimaging whereas Recommendation 2 focuses on a detailed restaging, including disappeared metastases mapping, and a strategic surgical approach.

Case-tailoring concordance: The recommendations differ in case-specific details, such as the emphasis in Recommendation 2 on the status of the rectal tumor and specific surgical approaches, while Recommendation 1 focuses on potential techniques like PVE or ALPPS and specific chemotherapy regimens based on molecular status.

Missing data concordance: There are discrepancies in the missing data identified by each recommendation. Recommendation 1 emphasizes hepatic anatomical details, liver function tests, and chemotherapy history, while Recommendation 2 focuses on mapping disappeared lesions and incorporates advanced factors like ctDNA analysis. They do not identify the same set of missing information.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The patient has residual hepatic disease (six stable lesions and one 5 cm progressing lesion in segment VII) after systemic therapy.  
- Definitive determination of resectability requires:  
  • Precise anatomic mapping of all remaining lesions (segmental location, size, proximity to major vessels or biliary structures).  
  • Quantitative assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) and hepatic functional reserve (ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh).  
  • Confirmation that the primary colon tumor is controlled or resectable.  
- The progressing lesion suggests chemo‑resistance and will likely need a local ablative or down‑staging maneuver before a curative‑intent hepatectomy can be contemplated.  
- Because these critical pieces of information are absent, immediate curative surgery cannot be planned, but the disease may become resectable after targeted interventions.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic chemotherapy with a regimen active in KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI combined with bevacizumab). Aim for further tumor shrinkage and control of the progressing segment VII lesion.  
- Evaluate response after 2–3 additional cycles with high‑quality contrast‑enhanced MRI or triphasic CT.  
- For the 5 cm segment VII lesion that is progressing:  
  • If it remains >3 cm after additional chemotherapy, plan a locoregional approach (percutaneous microwave/RFA, irreversible electroporation, or stereotactic body radiotherapy) to achieve local control.  
  • Consider portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right liver if resection would leave an insufficient FLR after removal of right‑sided lesions.  
- Re‑assess the six stable lesions after systemic therapy and/or local treatment:  
  • If all lesions can be encompassed within an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection leaving ≥30 % FLR (≥40 % in steatotic liver) and R0 margins are achievable, proceed to curative hepatectomy (single‑stage if feasible, otherwise two‑stage with PVE or ALPPS).  
- Manage the primary left‑sided colon cancer:  
  • If not yet resected, schedule a colectomy either before or after hepatic surgery, depending on symptomatology and overall fitness.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy should be continued according to standard guidelines for stage IV disease with curative resection.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact size, segmental location, and vascular/biliary relationship of each of the six stable hepatic lesions.  
- Quantitative liver volumetry and calculation of future liver remnant.  
- Baseline hepatic functional assessment (Child‑Pugh, ICG clearance, MELD).  
- Current status of the primary colon tumor (resected, symptomatic, or still present).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Details of the chemotherapy regimen already administered, number of cycles, and toxicity profile.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that may affect surgical risk.  
- Tumor marker trends (CEA, CA 19‑9) to gauge systemic response.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
The two recommendations differ significantly across all evaluation criteria:

1. **Completeness:** Recommendation 1 considers the case potentially resectable with criteria for resectability including precise anatomic mapping and FLR assessment, while Recommendation 2 explicitly labels it as unresectable at this stage, though it does mention the possibility of selective local strategies. Recommendation 1 provides a detailed plan involving systemic therapy, locoregional treatment, and potential curative resection, while Recommendation 2 suggests systemic strategy reassessment and the possibility of cytoreductive rather than curative intent surgery.

2. **Step Concordance:** In Step 1, Recommendation 1 considers the situation potentially resectable with further interventions, whereas Recommendation 2 clearly deems it currently unresectable but suggests local strategies. In Step 2, the management plans diverge with Recommendation 1 aiming for curative resection post additional systemic and local therapies, while Recommendation 2 prioritizes regaining systemic control and adopts a cytoreductive approach.

3. **Case-Tailoring Concordance:** Recommendation 1 accounts for the KRAS-mutated status in its systemic therapy choice, whereas Recommendation 2 does not mention mutation-specific therapy but refers to a potential adaptation of systemic therapy. Furthermore, Recommendation 2 adds the need for molecular profiling and addresses potential implications for adjuvant therapy. 

4. **Missing Data Concordance:** Both recommendations identify the need for exact lesion mapping and FLR assessment, but differ in other data needs. Recommendation 1 focuses on tumor marker trends and detailed systemic therapy history, while Recommendation 2 emphasizes molecular profiles, liquid biopsies, and uses of ctDNA and CTCs, which Recommendation 1 does not mention.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient shows a radiologic complete response after 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, but definitive surgical planning requires (a) high‑sensitivity liver imaging (gadoxetate‑enhanced MRI or PET‑CT) to exclude occult residual hepatic disease and (b) definitive staging of the primary rectal tumor (MRI pelvis, endoscopic assessment) to determine need for neoadjuvant radiotherapy or surgical resection. Until these decisive data are obtained, resection cannot be confirmed as upfront feasible.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain a liver‑specific MRI (gadoxetate‑enhanced) and a whole‑body PET‑CT to confirm absence of residual hepatic or extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Perform a thorough rectal work‑up: high‑resolution pelvic MRI, endoscopic evaluation, and assessment of clinical response; determine whether the primary lesion requires neoadjuvant chemoradiation or can proceed directly to surgery.  
- If imaging confirms no residual liver disease and the primary tumor is resectable without further radiotherapy, plan a curative‑intent resection of the rectal cancer (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection as indicated).  
- During the colorectal operation, conduct intra‑operative liver ultrasound; if any suspicious foci are identified, perform a parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy or wedge resection to obtain pathology.  
- If intra‑operative assessment confirms a true complete hepatic response, no liver resection is performed; the patient is managed with surveillance.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant therapy is guided by final pathology (e.g., consider additional systemic therapy if high‑risk features are present).  
- Implement a strict surveillance protocol: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed staging of the primary rectal tumor (T stage, N stage, distance from mesorectal fascia, response to chemotherapy).  
- Current status of the primary lesion (size, ulceration, mucosal involvement) and need for radiotherapy.  
- Baseline liver function and future liver remnant assessment (Child‑Pugh, ICG clearance, volumetry).  
- Results of high‑resolution liver MRI and/or PET‑CT after chemotherapy.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status).

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Single 3.9 cm lesion confined to segment VII, no extra‑hepatic disease on imaging.  
- Prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V leaves sufficient future liver remnant (segments II‑III, VI, VII‑VIII, I) to accommodate a segmentectomy or wedge resection of VII.  
- No vascular invasion described; lesion is anatomically approachable.  
- KRAS mutation influences systemic therapy choice but not surgical feasibility.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative work‑up:  
  • Verify liver synthetic function (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and volumetric CT/MRI to confirm FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if steatosis/fibrosis).  
  • Assess performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and cardiopulmonary fitness.  
- Surgical plan:  
  • Proceed to curative‑intent liver resection – anatomical segmentectomy of VII or non‑anatomic wedge resection with ≥ 5 mm margin, using intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude occult disease.  
  • Employ low‑central venous pressure anesthesia to minimize blood loss.  
- Post‑operative oncologic management:  
  • Initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy within 6‑8 weeks (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX; consider adding bevacizumab given KRAS‑mutated disease if not contraindicated).  
  • No routine radiotherapy for isolated liver recurrence.  
- Surveillance:  
  • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years, then every 6‑12 months up to 5 years.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- No essential data are lacking to make a reliable resection and treatment recommendation.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver metastasis in segment VII (3.9 cm) after a prior bisegmentectomy IV–V, without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesion is located in a posterior segment and appears anatomically accessible while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and functional reserve. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior limited hepatectomy, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of segment VII.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (current liver) and confirm preservation of portal inflow and hepatic venous outflow.

B. Consider peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the KRAS mutation and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered to address potential micrometastatic disease.

C. Close radiologic reassessment

Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has four bilobar liver metastases, which can be addressed with modern two‑stage or ALPPS strategies, but one lesion in segment VII invades the inferior vena cava over a 1 cm segment. Resection would require IVC segmental resection and reconstruction, a high‑complexity procedure that can be performed only after confirming:  
- the exact circumferential extent of IVC involvement and the presence of adequate collateral venous drainage,  
- that a sufficient future liver remnant (FLR) can be achieved (volumetric assessment, possible portal vein embolization), and  
- that the patient’s performance status and cardiopulmonary reserve permit a combined hepatic‑vascular operation.  
These prerequisites constitute a specific missing piece of information; therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy with a doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type status; aim for 2–3 months of treatment to assess tumor biology and potential down‑staging.  
- Re‑image the liver (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) after chemotherapy to evaluate response of all lesions, especially the IVC‑invading metastasis, and to perform volumetric analysis of the FLR.  
- If the IVC involvement remains limited (<50 % circumferential, ≤1 cm length) and adequate collateral flow is demonstrated, plan a multidisciplinary operative approach:  
   • Stage 1: Right hepatectomy (including segment VII) with en‑bloc IVC segmental resection and interposition graft (e.g., PTFE or autologous vein) performed by hepatobiliary and cardiothoracic surgeons; simultaneously resect the primary left‑sided colon tumor or schedule it as a separate procedure depending on bowel preparation and patient condition.  
   • If FLR is <30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver, perform portal vein embolization (PVE) before or after the first hepatic resection to induce hypertrophy of the left lateral segments.  
   • Stage 2 (4–6 weeks later, after FLR hypertrophy and recovery): Completion left‑lateral segmentectomy or ablation of remaining lesions, aiming for R0 margins.  
- Throughout the treatment course, monitor CEA trends and assess for extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung, peritoneum) with CT chest/abdomen. If new extra‑hepatic sites appear or the IVC invasion proves unresectable, shift to systemic therapy alone or consider palliative locoregional options (radiofrequency ablation, stereotactic body radiotherapy).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and cardiopulmonary reserve (ejection fraction, pulmonary function).  
- Detailed vascular imaging describing the circumferential extent of IVC invasion, presence of collateral venous pathways, and relationship to hepatic veins.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, platelets, albumin).  
- Status of the primary left‑colon tumor (resected, symptomatic, or pending resection).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Results of portal venous assessment (patency, tumor involvement).  
These data are essential to confirm whether an R0 hepatic‑IVC resection with adequate FLR is feasible and safe.
